issues.legal_issue: A beneficiary whose interests may be substantially affected must be given an opportunity to be heard before the Government withdraws an acquisition in which possession has not been taken.
material_facts: The association was the beneficiary of the acquisition, which was intended to provide housing sites to its members.
The acquisition had progressed through the declaration, award and payment of the acquisition costs by the association.
The Government withdrew the acquisition without giving the association notice or an opportunity to be heard.
The landowners had a statutory route to claim compensation for damage or costs resulting from the acquisition, but no similar remedy was available to the beneficiary.
issues.conclusion: The Government could not withdraw the acquisition without first hearing the beneficiary; the withdrawal was vitiated because the association was not heard.
issues.legal_principle: Natural justice is ordinarily read into a statutory power unless excluded expressly or by necessary implication. Under Union of India v. Col. J.N. Sinha, Olga Tellis v. Bombay Municipal Corporation and C.B. Gautam v. Union of India, the ordinary rule is that a person likely to be affected must have an opportunity to be heard, and the party asserting an exception bears the burden of establishing it. Section 48(1) of the Land Acquisition Act did not exclude a beneficiary’s hearing. The distinction between a landowner, whose interests are addressed by Section 48(2), and a beneficiary was recognized in Amar Nath Ashram Trust Society v. Governor of U.P., Special Land Acquisition Officer v. Godrej & Boyce and Larsen & Toubro Ltd. v. State of Gujarat.

rule.if: appeal_challenges_acquisition_withdrawal and beneficiary_materially_affected and acquisition_steps_substantially_advanced and beneficiary_not_heard

predicates.appeal_challenges_acquisition_withdrawal: The proceeding challenges a government decision to withdraw an acquisition before possession has been taken.
predicates.beneficiary_materially_affected: The proposed withdrawal may cause substantial loss to the person or body for whose benefit the acquisition was undertaken.
predicates.acquisition_steps_substantially_advanced: The acquisition has proceeded through substantial formal steps, and the beneficiary has incurred costs toward it.
predicates.beneficiary_not_heard: The government withdrew the acquisition without giving the beneficiary notice or an opportunity to present its position.

issues.definition: When a challenged withdrawal may substantially affect a beneficiary after the acquisition has substantially advanced, the beneficiary must be heard before withdrawal if no hearing was given.

issues.legal_issue: The Government’s discretion to withdraw an acquisition is reviewable and cannot be exercised arbitrarily or upheld on reasons different from those on which the decision was made.
material_facts: The withdrawal notification gave no reason for withdrawing the acquisition.
The State later relied on an objection that the association was not eligible to sponsor the housing scheme because of its registered objects.
The association remained registered, and some of its objects fell within the objects permitted by the applicable state registration law.
The objection to the association’s registration and the public-purpose basis had been considered and rejected before the final declaration of acquisition.
The owners had challenged the final declaration but withdrew their challenge.
The record showed that a local legislator had written to the Revenue Department seeking withdrawal on behalf of the landowners.
issues.conclusion: The State’s discretion was not absolute or immune from review. The stated basis for withdrawal was unacceptable, and the State could not support the decision with a different ground later; the withdrawal was arbitrary and invalid.
issues.legal_principle: Amar Nath Ashram Trust Society v. Governor of U.P., approved in Larsen & Toubro Ltd. v. State of Gujarat, holds that a decision to withdraw an acquisition may be challenged as mala fide or arbitrary and that the State’s discretion is not absolute. Under Mohinder Singh Gill v. Chief Election Commissioner, an order must be judged by the reasons on which it was made and cannot be supplemented by new reasons in an affidavit. The Court also held that, once a declaration under Section 6(3) treated the land as needed for a public purpose, that issue could not be reopened by the State or by owners who had withdrawn their challenge to the declaration.

rule.if: appeal_challenges_acquisition_withdrawal and withdrawal_decision_reviewable and withdrawal_basis_incorrect and withdrawal_notice_gives_no_reason

predicates.appeal_challenges_acquisition_withdrawal: The proceeding challenges a government decision to withdraw an acquisition before possession has been taken.
predicates.withdrawal_decision_reviewable: The government’s decision to withdraw the acquisition is challenged as arbitrary or otherwise unlawful.
predicates.withdrawal_basis_incorrect: The ground relied on for withdrawal conflicts with established facts or with an issue already finally determined in the acquisition proceedings.
predicates.withdrawal_notice_gives_no_reason: The withdrawal notification itself states no reason for the decision.

issues.definition: If a challenged withdrawal is reviewable, rests on an incorrect basis and its notice gives no reason, the withdrawal is invalid as arbitrary.

issues.legal_issue: An acquisition for a registered society’s housing scheme may qualify as a public purpose where the required prior government approval is given and the society has a housing scheme for which land is sought.
material_facts: The association was registered under the applicable state societies registration law, and its registration had not been cancelled.
Some of the association’s stated objects fell within the objects permitted by that law.
The association submitted a housing scheme, including a layout plan, proposed sites, membership and allotment details, and information about financing and administration.
The Town Planning Authority’s clearance was obtained, and the relevant authorities examined the proposal and found its particulars satisfactory.
The Government’s letter of 15 March 1991 conveyed approval to initiate acquisition for the association’s housing scheme.
The final declaration stated that the acquisition was for the public purpose of providing housing sites to the association’s members.
issues.conclusion: The acquisition was properly initiated as a public-purpose acquisition for the association’s housing scheme. The Court did not need to decide whether there was a conflict between the central and state registration provisions or which would prevail under Article 254 of the Constitution.
issues.legal_principle: Section 3(f)(vi) of the Land Acquisition Act requires prior approval of the appropriate Government, land for a housing scheme, and sponsorship by a society registered under the Societies Registration Act, 1860 or corresponding state law. Sections 4(1) and 6 govern the public-purpose acquisition process, and Section 6(3) makes the declaration conclusive evidence that the land is needed for a public purpose. The Court held that Article 166’s requirements are directory and that government action may be established as a matter of fact: Chitralekha v. State of Mysore, Dattatreya v. State of Bombay and Major E.G. Barsay v. State of Bombay. Gulabra v. State of Gujarat was distinguishable on its facts. The Court found the approval and scheme established on the record and did not decide the Article 254 issue.

rule.if: acquisition_for_society_housing_scheme and society_registered_and_registration_uncancelled and housing_scheme_submitted and government_prior_approval_given

predicates.acquisition_for_society_housing_scheme: The acquisition is sought to provide land for a housing scheme sponsored by a society.
predicates.society_registered_and_registration_unca: The society is registered under an applicable registration law, and its registration has not been cancelled.
predicates.housing_scheme_submitted: The society has submitted details of a housing scheme, including its proposed layout and arrangements for allotment and administration.
predicates.government_prior_approval_given: The Government approved the acquisition for the housing scheme before the relevant acquisition notification was issued.

issues.definition: When a registered society submits a housing scheme and the Government gives prior approval for land to carry it out, the acquisition qualifies as one for a public purpose.

issues.legal_issue: Material collected during earlier acquisition efforts may be relied on for a later acquisition and approval if that material remains sufficient, relevant and genuine.
material_facts: Earlier acquisition notifications did not lead to a timely final declaration, so fresh notifications were issued.
The association’s scheme, membership, layout and other particulars had been examined by officials and committees during the earlier proceedings.
The Government considered the existing material when approving the later acquisition, and the record showed a detailed examination of the proposal.
The earlier notifications had not been cancelled; the proceedings could not continue under them because of administrative delay and the statutory time limit.
issues.conclusion: The expiry of the earlier proceedings did not erase the underlying material as a matter of fact, and the Government could rely on that material for the later acquisition and approval because it was sufficient, relevant and genuine.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 4(1) and 3(f)(vi) of the Land Acquisition Act do not prescribe the material on which the Government must base its preliminary view of public purpose or its prior approval. Under M/s Fomento Resorts and Hotels Ltd. v. Gustavo Renato D’Cruz Pinto, the Government may act on an independent inquiry, reports or information received, or an application by the beneficiary. There is no prohibition on using material already on record if it is sufficient, relevant and genuine. State of Gujarat v. Patel Chaturbhai Narsibhai was distinguishable because it concerned a cancelled notification and statutory requirements for acquisition for a company under Part VII.

predicates.later_acquisition_follows_earlier_time_b: A later acquisition is pursued after earlier proceedings could not continue within the applicable time limit.
predicates.earlier_material_examined: Officials or committees examined information about the beneficiary and its proposed scheme during the earlier proceedings.
predicates.earlier_material_sufficient_relevant_gen: The material remains adequate, relevant to the proposed acquisition and genuine when the Government considers the later proceedings.

issues.definition: When a later acquisition follows time-barred earlier proceedings and the material examined in those proceedings remains sufficient, relevant and genuine, that material may support the later acquisition.

issues.legal_issue: An acquisition pursued as a public-purpose acquisition under Part II is not subject to the separate procedures for acquisition for a company under Part VII merely because earlier administrative correspondence referred to company-acquisition procedures.
material_facts: The later notifications expressly described the acquisition as being for a public purpose and for the association’s housing scheme.
The acquisition was processed through the public-purpose inquiry and recommendation process, including review by district and state committees.
There was no evidence that the acquisition was in fact continued as an acquisition for a company under Part VII.
The respondents’ Part VII contention rested on internal correspondence, while the final acquisition documents and the proceedings treated the matter as a Part II acquisition.
issues.conclusion: The acquisition was initiated and continued under Part II, not Part VII, and the respondents’ contention that it followed a hybrid procedure was erroneous.
issues.legal_principle: Part II of the Land Acquisition Act governs acquisition for public purposes. Part VII, including Sections 38-A to 44-B and Section 39, requires prior government consent and an agreement for acquisition for a company. The Court distinguished State of Gujarat v. Patel Chaturbhai Narsibhai and Amar Nath Ashram Trust Society v. Governor of U.P. by reference to the records and the manner in which the acquisition was initiated and continued.

predicates.acquisition_notifications_state_public_p: The acquisition notifications identify a public purpose as the reason for acquiring the land.
predicates.acquisition_processed_as_public_purpose: The acquisition was examined and advanced through the procedures used for a public-purpose acquisition.
predicates.no_evidence_of_company_acquisition: The record does not establish that the acquisition was pursued for a company under a separate company-acquisition procedure.

issues.definition: When the notifications and proceedings identify a public purpose and the record does not establish a company acquisition, the acquisition proceeds under the public-purpose framework.
